messages:
Sam: Heads-up — Acme POC kickoff Monday. They want a Private/VPC path to our Private deployment. Need clear options for PrivateLink vs peering, how to preserve client IP, TLS‑inspect compatibility, required firewall allowlist (IPs/ports), and any pricing uplift. Who can take network + pricing asks?
Alex: I can take network. Quick notes: PrivateLink (interface endpoint) = our service exposed as ENIs in customer VPC, easy for onramp, avoids peering. VPC peering = full L3, preserves original src IPs but needs routing + peering limits. Tradeoffs:
- PrivateLink: easier security posture, limited cross-VPC visibility, NAT may change src IP unless we run proxy in customer VPC.
- Peering: more operational work, but you get src IP preservation and simpler MTU.
Sam: Customer insists on preserving client IP for downstream logging/ACLs. Is that a blocker for PrivateLink?
Alex: With standard AWS Interface Endpoint -> traffic goes to our service ENI; source becomes the customer's ENI private IP. If they NAT out (eg via egress NAT GW) the public egress IP will be our captured source. To truly preserve original public client IP to our backend you need either:
1) VPC peering (traffic stays 1:1 L3) OR
2) run a small NAT/proxy near their clients that forwards X-Forwarded-For to our service (we accept XFF) OR
3) deploy Redwood Private inside their VPC (customer-managed) so we see original src.
Maria: Pricing note: Private deployments have a platform licensing component + infra. Static EIP usage / BYOIP for dedicated egress can add a small infra fee. For a short POC we usually absorb minimal infra costs but document any sustained BYOIP/EIP needs upfront :money_with_wings:.
Raj: TLS inspect: if the customer's outbound proxy is doing TLS inspection, it may break SNI and cert validation. Options:
- Recommend SNI passthrough (no MITM) for calls to Redwood endpoints.
- If they must TLS-inspect, provide IP allowlist so the inspection appliance can skip MITM for those IPs.
- Alternatively, use mTLS or client certs depending on deployment.
Alex: For firewall allowlist, minimal outbound requirements are just HTTPS (443) to Redwood egress IPs + DNS. Example snippet for customer firewall team: 
```
# Allow outbound to Redwood POC endpoints
Allow TCP 443 -> 52.203.45.16/32  # redwood-poc-1
Allow TCP 443 -> 52.203.45.17/32  # redwood-poc-2
Allow UDP 53   -> your-resolver-ip  # DNS
```
(We'll provide the definitive IP list; if they use PrivateLink they can allow the interface endpoint ENIs instead.)
Pete: POC checklist from SE side: please ask customer for:
- Source CIDR(s) for onramp
- Whether they require src IP preservation or X-Forwarded-For is OK
- Any TLS inspection appliances / proxies in path
- Expected RPS and typical payload size (so we can advise Hosted vs Dedicated capacity)
- Contractual need for BYOIP / static egress IPs
OpsBot: Provisioning note: created temporary preview endpoint for Acme POC -> https://preview-1715554444.redwood.example (expires in 14 days).
Sam: Great. Raj — can you confirm if security questionnaire will accept "provide SOC reports + KMS/HSM integration details" or they specifically ask for on‑prem HSM?
Raj: I'll check. Short answer: we support KMS integrations and customer-managed keys for Private deployments; for air-gapped HSM we need an enterprise migration plan — flagging as potential blocker for regulated customers.
Alex: I'll prepare a one‑page network diagram (PrivateLink vs peering) + the firewall snippet and send to Sam/SE. Ping me if they want a quick call tomorrow.
Sam: Thanks team — I'll loop in the customer's network contact and share the doc once ready. :thumbsup:
